### Inference vs training in a systolic array

| | Inference | Training |
|---|-----------|----------|
| Dataflow | **Weight-stationary** (each PE holds a weight; activations flow through) | No single dominant dataflow |
| Matmuls per layer | 1 (forward only) | 3 (1 forward + 2 backward: dA = dY·Wᵀ, dW = Xᵀ·dY) |
| MACs per layer | N³ (= 2·N³ FLOPs) | 3·N³ MACs (= 6·N³ FLOPs) |
| Memory | Weight memory bandwidth dominant cost (batch = 1 to few) | Must also store forward activations X for dW |
| Examples | Many ASICs | TPU/Trainium use weight-stationary forward, different backward tiling; Eyeriss prefers output/row-stationary |

## 1. Why In-Memory Computing? — The Energy Problem

### Memory access dominates energy
At 45-nm (Verma et al., 2019), accessing a 64-bit word costs:
- **8 kB SRAM**: ~10 pJ
- **32 kB SRAM**: ~20 pJ
- **100 MB**: ~100 pJ
- **DRAM**: **~2,000 pJ (2 nJ)**

Compare to the actual multiply:
- FP32 MULT: ~5 pJ
- INT32 MULT: ~3 pJ
- INT8 MULT: ~0.3 pJ
- INT4 MULT: ~0.1 pJ

**DRAM access is ~20,000× more expensive than an INT4 multiply.** The moment a model's weights don't fit in SRAM, energy is dominated by data movement, not computation. This is the core motivation for IMC.

### Conventional vs computational memory
- **Conventional (von Neumann)**: data D flows over a digital interface to the processing unit; the unit computes f(D) and returns the result.
- **In-memory (computational memory)**: a command "perform f on D" is sent to the memory; the memory array itself produces f(D). Eliminates the bulk data transfer.

### Memory types used for IMC
| | Charge-based | Resistance-based |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | SRAM, DRAM, Flash | RRAM, PCM, STT-MRAM |
| Mechanism | Stored charge | Programmable resistance |

| Property | RRAM | PCM | STT-MRAM |
|----------|------|-----|----------|
| Mechanism | Filament formation | Phase change | Magnetic spin torque |
| Write speed | ~10 ns | ~50–100 ns | ~2–10 ns |
| Endurance | 10⁶–10¹² | 10⁶–10⁸ | >10¹² |
| Analog (MLC) | Strong | Strong | Limited |
| Maturity | Research/production | Research/early prod. | Production (embedded) |

> **MLC** = Multi-Level Cell (stores more than 1 bit per device).

### IMC vs non-IMC payoff
Verma et al. show **~10× to 1000× gains** in both throughput (GOP/s/mm²) and energy efficiency (TOP/s/W) when moving the same neural network workload from non-IMC to IMC silicon.

### How mature is IMC? (TRL 7–8 / 9)
- **Software IMC** (Mature): In-memory databases keep the working dataset in RAM instead of on disk. SAP HANA, Oracle TimesTen, Redis, Apache Ignite. DRAM holds 66.7% of IMC spend (2024).
- **Digital CIM** (Early commercial): UPMEM PIM-DRAM shipping; Samsung HBM-PIM and Micron CXL DIMMs in trials. INT4/INT8 CIM macros at 22–25 TOPS/W.
- **Analog IMC** (Pre-commercial): IBM AIMC prototypes for LLMs; Mythic, Aspinity at edge AI. Challenges remain: analog noise, precision, scaling to billion-parameter models.

Market: $16.3B (2024) → $46.9B by 2033 at 12.5% CAGR; AI inference is the key growth driver.

## 2. The Crossbar Primitive — Analog MVM in O(1) Time

A resistive crossbar performs a matrix-vector multiplication **in a single read cycle** by using two universal circuit laws:

- **Ohm's law**: I(i,j) = G(i,j) · V(i)
- **Kirchhoff's current law**: I(j) = Σᵢ G(i,j) · V(i)

In matrix form: **I = G·V**, evidencing the multiplication of conductance matrix G with voltage vector v. One column current = one dot product. Whole MVM in a single read cycle.

### Mapping an NN layer onto a crossbar
- Weights W → conductances G(i,j) programmed into resistive memory cells (ReRAM, PCM)
- Input vector → voltages V(i) applied on the rows
- Output current per column = Σᵢ G(i,j)·V(i) = the dot product for that output neuron

This works because **parallel multiplication** happens at each intersection (one resistive junction per weight) and **current summation** happens automatically on each bitline via Kirchhoff's law.

For training (backward pass), the conductance matrix is read in the opposite direction so the system computes Wᵀ · δ — useful for backprop error propagation.

### Capacitive variant
Same idea but with **capacitances C(i,j)** instead of conductances. Total charge accumulated at the j-th bitline: Q(j) = Σᵢ C(i,j) · V(i). Avoids static leakage during MVM.

### Crosspoint cell structures
1. **1R** (one resistor) — passive resistive cell, simplest, suffers sneak paths
2. **1S1R** (one selector + one resistor) — nonlinear selector blocks sneak paths without losing density
3. **1T1R** (one transistor + one resistor) — best per-cell selectivity, lower density
4. **1C** (one capacitor) — capacitive variant, no static leakage

### Static vs Dynamic IMC

| Static IMC (low-voltage regime) | Dynamic IMC (switching regime) |
|---|---|
| Matrix-vector multiplication | Supervised training |
| Inverse matrix-vector multiplication | Spike-based learning |
| Content-addressable memory | Stateful logic |
| Combinatorial optimization | True random number generator |
| Physical unclonable function | |
| Bayesian inference | |

## 3. Sneak Paths in Crossbars (CF06 connection)

**Sneak paths** = unintended current pathways through unselected cells in a memory array. When you try to read one cell, current can flow through neighboring cells via the shared rows and columns, corrupting the read.

Why it matters for MVM:
- The intended signal is the current through one selected cell (representing weight × input)
- Sneak currents through floating rows/columns add to the sensed current
- The sense amplifier can't tell signal from sneak — every dot product gets corrupted
- In a large array, every floating node adds more sneak loops; errors compound across all the dot products read at the same time

**Solutions**:
- **Diodes** at each cell to enforce unidirectional current
- **1T1R structures** — to read/write a cell, raise only that row's word line V_GX, turning on only that row's transistors. Transistors in every other row are off, so no sneak current can flow.

This is exactly the CF06 CMAN problem (`codefest/cf06/cman_sneak_path.md`).

## 4. Sparse MVM and the Sparse-on-Crossbar Problem

### What is sparse MVM?
**y = A·x where A is mostly zeros.** Real workloads:
- GNNs, recommender systems, scientific PDEs: 90–99% zero
- Storing/multiplying zeros wastes memory, bandwidth, energy
- Compressed formats (CSR, CSC, COO) skip zeros entirely

### Naïve sparse-on-crossbar fails
Mapping a sparse matrix straight onto an 8×8 crossbar: only 8/64 cells used (~13%). What goes wrong:
- **Area**: every zero still consumes a programmed cell and wire pitch
- **Energy**: bitlines charge through all cells, including zero conductances
- **Accuracy**: many tiny currents sum on each bitline, ADC range wasted on noise
- **Tile size fixed** (e.g. 128×128): large matrices need many tiles

### Solution: pack non-zeros densely
1. **Permute & pack** (software) — reorder rows and columns so non-zeros cluster into dense blocks. Map each block to a small tile.
   - Example: 8 non-zeros, 64 cells → 9 cells (7× smaller)
2. **Tile partitioning** (software) — split A into k×k sub-matrices; skip all-zero tiles entirely.
3. **Row & bitline gating** (hardware) — power-gate rows whose input is zero and columns with no non-zeros. Cuts both dynamic and leakage energy with no accuracy cost.
4. **Format-aware drivers** (hardware) — stream x in CSR/CSC order; drive only rows that match active non-zero patterns in each tile.

### CSR — Compressed Sparse Row
Three arrays for a sparse matrix:
- `values[]` — the non-zeros
- `col_idx[]` — column index of each non-zero
- `row_ptr[]` — where each row's run of non-zeros starts in `values` (length N+1, not nnz)

To read row i: slice `row_ptr[i]..row_ptr[i+1]` gives all non-zeros in row i. Memory: ~2·nnz + N values instead of N². Walks rows in order → ideal for y = A·x.

**CSR vs COO**: COO stores (row, col, val) for every NZ → 3·nnz entries. CSR run-length-encodes the row coordinate into `row_ptr`.

### When does sparse on crossbar pay off?
- **High sparsity** (≥90% zeros): analog savings dominate the digital decoder cost
- **Structured sparsity** (block / N:M patterns): simpler decoder
- **Weight reuse**: amortizes overhead across many uses
- **Large matrices**: overhead is O(NZ), savings are O(N²)

**Crossover**: below ~70% sparsity, a dense crossbar usually wins — the decoder + scheduler + irregular access cost more than the zeros you skipped.

## 5. Neuromorphic Chips — What They Are

> **Neuromorphic chips are specialized hardware designed to mimic the structure and function of the human brain.** Unlike traditional computing architectures, these chips are built to process information in ways similar to biological neural networks.

**Cerebras WSE-3 is *not* neuromorphic** despite being huge. It's a wafer-scale GPU/accelerator for LLM training/inference, not a brain-inspired chip.

### Key characteristics of all neuromorphic chips
| Feature | Traditional | Neuromorphic |
|---------|------------|--------------|
| Architecture | Von Neumann (separate memory and processing) | Brain-inspired (integrated memory and processing) |
| Processing | Sequential, clock-driven | Parallel, event-driven |
| Power consumption | High | Low to very low |
| Learning | Requires separate algorithms | Often incorporates on-chip learning |
| Precision | High precision arithmetic | Variable/lower precision, stochastic |
| Fault tolerance | Limited | High (distributed processing) |
| Specialization | General-purpose | Specialized for pattern recognition, sensor processing |

### Four pillars
1. **Parallel processing** — computation and memory integrated in the same physical structures (similar to biological neurons)
2. **Event-driven computation** — operate on "spikes" rather than continuous clock cycles, energy only consumed when processing
3. **Adaptability** — on-chip learning mechanisms (synaptic plasticity)
4. **Distributed memory** — information stored across the network in connection strengths, not in a centralized memory

### Different approaches
- **Direct silicon neurons** (Loihi, TrueNorth)
- **Simulated neurons on specialized processors** (SpiNNaker — ARM cores running neuron models)
- **Analog / Digital / Mixed-signal** implementations

### The trade-off spectrum
```
SpiNNaker ── Akida/Loihi/BrainScaleS-2 ── IBM TrueNorth/NorthPole
   ↑                ↑                              ↑
Flexibility ───────────────────────────────► Performance
More digital                            More analog (but needs DAC/ADC)
```

Other trade-off axes (per Borghi et al. review):
- **State architecture**: Digital (Xylo, TrueNorth, Loihi, Akida, SpiNNaker2) vs mixed-signal/analog (DYNAP-SE2, T1)
- **Weight implementation**: Routing-based (Xylo, Loihi, SpiNNaker2) vs crossbar (T1, TrueNorth, HERMES)
- **Learning**: Off-chip (Speck, Xylo) vs on-chip (Loihi, SpiNNaker2)
- **Compute/memory**: Compute-near-memory (Speck, Xylo, Loihi) vs compute-in-memory (TrueNorth, T1, HERMES)
- **Application focus**: Edge/online (Speck, Xylo, T1, Syntiant, Akida) vs data-center/offline (Loihi, SpiNNaker2)

## 6. Communication: AER + Network-on-Chip

### Address Event Representation (AER)
Spike-event message-passing protocol used by virtually all neuromorphic chips:
- When a neuron spikes, the system sends only the **spiking neuron's address** as an event packet
- Only active neurons generate messages — sparse, event-driven, asynchronous
- Timing information is **implicit** in when the message is sent
- Each spike encoded as a packet: `| DEST_CORE | NEURON_ID | TIMESTAMP |`

> The simplest and most efficient AER implementation sends a firing neuron's unique ID to all nodes containing any of that neuron's targets.

### Network-on-Chip (NoC)
Packet-switched interconnect for many-core and neuromorphic chips. Replaces buses and point-to-point wires.

**Components**:
- **Router**: arbitration, buffering, switching
- **Link**: physical wires between routers
- **NI** (Network Interface): packs/unpacks data

**Why use it**:
- Scalability — bandwidth grows with router count
- Parallelism — multiple concurrent transactions
- Modularity — drop-in IP blocks exist

Common topology: **2D mesh** (each node = router + processing core). Others: torus, ring, tree, butterfly, hierarchical.

### AER over NoC — how it actually flows
1. Neuron spikes → emits only its own address (it's "dumb" — knows only its own ID)
2. Local SRAM **routing table** at the source core looks up the synaptic fan-out: src → [dest list]
3. Network interface emits one packet per destination (1 spike → N packets)
4. Routers forward by DEST coordinates (XY routing, etc.)

**Connectivity = table**: synapses live in SRAM, not in wires. Rewriting the table rewires the network. Fan-out at source enables on-line learning (STDP).

Real chips:
- **SpiNNaker**: multicast routers
- **Loihi**: axon table
- **TrueNorth**: per-neuron destination list

## 7. Major Neuromorphic Chips

### SpiNNaker (Univ. of Manchester)
- **Approach**: simulate neurons on general-purpose ARM cores
- **SpiNNaker1** (130nm CMOS): ~1 million ARM9 cores across 1,200 boards
- **SpiNNaker2** (22nm FDSOI): aims for 10M cores; current implementation ~5.2M cores across 720 boards; ~144 ARM M4F per chip, 18 MB SRAM, 8 GB DRAM PoP package
- **Node**: 18 ARM968 cores (1 spare), each with 96 kB local memory + 128 MB shared SDRAM, packet router
- Each core: 200 MHz, 32-bit integer, no FPU → fixed-point arithmetic
- Software: SC&MP (Spinnaker Control & Monitor Program), SARK (Spinnaker Application Runtime Kernel), Spin1 API; real-time event-driven model

### IBM TrueNorth (2015)
- **65 mW, 5.4 billion transistors** real-time neurosynaptic processor
- 4,096 neurosynaptic cores → **1 million digital neurons + 256 million synapses**
- Event-driven routing, non-von Neumann, low-power, defect-tolerant
- Asynchronous router; synchronous neuron + SRAM controller; QDI (Quasi-Delay-Insensitive) async circuits with handshaking
- Per-tick computation (1 kHz sync trigger):
  1. Core receives spikes, stores in input buffers
  2. On tick, spikes distributed across horizontal axons
  3. Where synapse exists between axon and dendrite, spike delivered to neuron
  4. Each neuron integrates incoming spikes, updates membrane potential
  5. Leak value subtracted from membrane potential
  6. If potential exceeds threshold → spike, sent into network
- Neuron block: **augmented integrate-and-fire** (simpler than Hodgkin-Huxley or Izhikevich)
- Includes pseudo-random number generator for stochastic spike integration
- 5 elements per neuron: Leak Unit, Synapse Unit, Integrator Unit, Threshold and Reset Unit, Leak Reversal Unit
- 2D mesh router with 6 processes (from local, forward E/W/N/S, to local)

### IBM NorthPole (2023)
Architecture and programming model for neural inference, built on **10 interrelated, synergistic axioms**:

1. **Specialized for neural inference**: no data-dependent conditional branching; no training or scientific computation
2. **Biological precision**: optimized for 8-, 4-, and 2-bit low-precision (sufficient for SOTA inference accuracy)
3. **Distributed core array**: 16×16 cores, each capable of **8192 2-bit operations per cycle**
4. **Distributed memory near and intertwined with compute** — exploits data locality for energy efficiency; large on-chip memory, not centralized
5. **Two dense NoCs** for compute/memory interconnect (inspired by long-distance white-matter and short-distance gray-matter brain pathways)
6. Two more NoCs for reconfiguring synaptic weights and programs
7. **Data-independent branching** → fully pipelined, stall-free, deterministic control. No memory misses → no speculative execution needed
8. **Co-optimized training algorithms** that incorporate low-precision constraints into training
9. **Codesigned software** (compiler, validator, runtime)
10. **Frame-based usage**: write input frame, read output frame; operates independently of attached general processor

**Performance highlight** (ResNet-50 inference, INT8/4/2): NorthPole achieves 42,460 FPS at 74 W on a 12 nm process with 22 billion transistors — competitive with H100 (81,292 FPS at 700 W on 4 nm with 80 billion transistors) on energy/space metrics.

### BrainScaleS / BrainScaleS-2 (Heidelberg University)
Analog mixed-signal, part of Human Brain Project.

| Feature | BrainScaleS-1 | BrainScaleS-2 |
|---------|---------------|---------------|
| Integration | Wafer-scale (384 HICANNs/wafer) | Single-chip ASIC |
| Neurons | Up to 196,608 per wafer | 512 per chip |
| Synapses | ~44 million per wafer | 212k–217k plastic per chip |
| Architecture | Mixed-signal (analog neurons + synapses) | Hybrid (analog core + digital processors) |
| Speed | **1,000–10,000× biological real-time** | 1,000× biological real-time |
| Process | 180 nm | 65 nm |
| Plasticity | Fixed models | **Programmable via PPU** (custom CPU) |
| Neuron model | Adaptive spiking | **Adaptive Exponential Integrate-and-Fire (AdEx)** |
| Programming | PyNN | PyNN |

**AdEx model**:
$$C_m \dot{V} = -g_l(V - E_l) + g_l \Delta_T \exp\!\left(\frac{V - V_T}{\Delta_T}\right) - w + I$$
$$\tau_w \dot{w} = a(V - E_L) - w$$

**Architecture**: synaptic crossbar (256 rows × 128 columns) per quadrant, with neuron circuits, analog parameter storage, two digital control/plasticity processors (PPU), and event routing network. Event packets get injected by synapse drivers into the synaptic crossbar; membrane voltage accumulates in neuron circuits and generates spikes.

### Loihi / Loihi 2 (Intel)

| Feature | Loihi (2017) | Loihi 2 (2021) |
|---------|--------------|----------------|
| Process | 14 nm | Intel 4 (pre-production) |
| Die size | 60 mm² | 31 mm² (about half) |
| Cores | 128 neuromorphic + 3 x86 | 128 neuromorphic + 6 Lakemont x86 |
| Neurons | ~130,000 | **Up to 1 million (~8×)** |
| Synapses | ~130M | Up to 120M |
| On-chip memory | >33 MB SRAM | ~25 MB SRAM |
| Neuron model | Fixed LIF | **Programmable via microcode** |
| Spike processing | Baseline | **Up to 10× faster** |
| Spike events | 1-bit (binary) | **Up to 32-bit graded spikes** |
| Connectivity | FPGA mediated | 10G Ethernet, GPIO, SPI |
| Framework | None at launch | **Lava** (open-source) |

**Loihi core microarchitecture**: SYNAPSE unit reads weights → DENDRITE unit updates compartment state variables (u, v) → SOMA generates spikes → AXON unit fans them out → LEARNING unit updates weights at epoch boundaries (reconfigurable learning engine).

**Loihi computational primitives**:
- **Stochastic noise**: pseudorandom values added to synaptic response, membrane voltage, refractory delay → supports Neural Sampling (probabilistic inference via Markov chain Monte Carlo)
- **Configurable synaptic, axon, refractory delays** → polychronous dynamics
- **Configurable dendritic tree processing** — neurons decomposed into compartment trees with programmable join functions
- **Neuron threshold adaptation** for intrinsic excitability homeostasis
- **Weight scaling/saturation** for "permanence" levels beyond inference range

**Loihi 2 implements**: discrete LIF model, complex-valued Resonate-and-Fire (RF), Resonate-and-Fire with Reset, Hopf Resonator (stable limit cycle, useful for spatiotemporal filtering and deep networks).

**LLM on Loihi 2** (ICLR 2025 workshop): MatMul-free LLM architecture adapted for Loihi 2 leverages low-precision, event-driven, stateful processing. 370M-parameter model quantized with no accuracy loss. Reports **up to 3× higher throughput with 2× less energy** vs transformer LLMs on edge GPU.

> Note: Loihi gives better energy-delay product on certain workloads (LASSO, graph search, k-NN, constraint satisfaction, sequential MNIST) but **is not in general competitive with general AI/ML workloads** (MobileNet, image segmentation).

### Akida (BrainChip, 2021)
- **First commercial neuromorphic processor** (commercially available since August 2021)
- Ultra-low-power, event-based processing, on-chip learning
- Supports CNNs, RNNs, and custom **Temporal Event-based Neural Networks (TENNs)** — combine spatial and temporal convolutions to process sequential spatiotemporal data
- 1.2M neurons, 10B synapses, very high power efficiency (sub-mW)
- Free chip emulator, TensorFlow-compatible MetaTF framework

## 9. Current Limitations and Challenges
- **Programming models**: lack of standardized frameworks (compare to CUDA's dominance for GPUs)
- **Application development**: limited software ecosystem vs traditional computing
- **Scaling**: hard to reach human-brain levels while maintaining efficiency
- **Algorithm mapping**: difficulty mapping existing AI algorithms to neuromorphic architectures (the "conversion or specialized training" challenge)
- **Adoption**: industry still in early research stages
- **Cost**: most neuromorphic chips rely on SRAM, which is ~2 orders of magnitude more expensive than DRAM

**Gaps in software ecosystem** (per Kudithipudi et al., Nature 2024):
- Mainstream AI: Nsight DL Designer → ONNX → TensorRT → optimized cloud deployment
- Neuromorphic: NEST Simulator → PyNN → ?? → no large-scale model runtime optimizations
- GNN tools: PyTorch ANN with PyG → TensorBoard analytics
- Neuromorphic equivalent (Norse SNN) missing libraries and analysis tools

## 11. The "AlexNet Moment" for Neuromorphic

Kudithipudi et al. (2024) argue neuromorphic computing is approaching its **AlexNet moment** — the breakthrough that catalyzes the field, analogous to AlexNet's 2012 ImageNet win that triggered the deep-learning revolution.

Just as AlexNet was enabled by GPU performance, a neuromorphic AlexNet moment could come from identifying the critical hardware requirements that unlock its potential. An initial breakthrough might emerge from a small hardware configuration (AlexNet used just two GPUs), inspiring larger-scale systems.

### Feature maturation timeline (NM at scale)

| Late stage ← → Early stage |
|--|
| **Sparse** (sparseness in activity/connectivity) |
| **Resource-aware** (memory/power/compute constraints) |
| **Scalable** (across many neural elements) |
| **Asynchronous** (event-driven communication) |
| **Distributed and hierarchical** |
| **Heterogeneous** (multiple platforms, sensors) |
| **Reconfigurable** (routing and configuration) |

Sparse and resource-aware are the most mature features; reconfigurability is the least.

### Progression of neuromorphic systems (neuron count over time)
- 1960: Perceptron MK1 — 520 neurons
- 1980s–90s: ETANN (128), MDAC (1,024), Silicon Retina (2,500)
- 2010s: CogniMem CM1K (102,000), Neurogrid (1M), BrainScaleS-1 (3.9M)
- 2014: TrueNorth (67M)
- 2015–2018: SpiNNaker (235M)
- 2020: Loihi (100M)
- 2021: Loihi 2 (1.15B)
- 2023+: SpiNNaker2 / SpiNNcloud (5.2B)

---

## 12. Open Question — Do We Need Brain-Like HW?

Borghi et al. (Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2024): brain's efficient fault-tolerant processing depends on **self-assembled and redundant** architectures, which are *not considered* in CMOS top-down roadmaps. The replication of these structures could enable performance benchmarks beyond conventional electronics in terms of compatibility and scalability.

This frames the larger question: can we keep extending CMOS-based neuromorphic chips, or do we need fundamentally new substrates (nanoparticle networks, self-assembled materials) to get true brain-like efficiency?

## Key Formulas

| Formula | Meaning |
|---------|---------|
| I(j) = Σᵢ G(i,j) · V(i) | Crossbar MVM via Ohm + Kirchhoff |
| I = G · V (matrix form) | Whole MVM in one read cycle |
| Q(j) = Σᵢ C(i,j) · V(i) | Capacitive crossbar variant |
| LIF: u[t] = λ·u[t-1] + a[t]; v[t] = λ·v[t-1] + u[t] | Loihi neuron model |
| C_m · dV/dt = -g_l(V-E_l) + g_l·Δ_T·exp((V-V_T)/Δ_T) - w + I | BrainScaleS-2 AdEx neuron |

## CMAN / CLLM Tie-Ins (for quiz prep)

- **CF06 CMAN — Sneak paths**: directly maps onto Sneak paths (1)–(4) slides in this deck. 1T1R structures and diodes are the standard solutions. The full 2×2 KCL analysis on a floating-node read is in `codefest/cf06/cman_sneak_path.md`.
- **CF06 CLLM — 4×4 crossbar MAC**: the crossbar primitive (analog MVM in one cycle) is what your binary-weight MAC is implementing in digital form. The "grid of wires with weights at intersections" framing from the spoken script maps 1:1 onto the resistive crossbar diagram here.
- **Project relevance** (K-Means PIM): the IMC maturity slide places **digital CIM** (the category your near-memory PIM chiplet falls into) at "Early Commercial" — UPMEM PIM-DRAM is the closest production analog. Your 16 TB/s HBM3 design is consistent with the Neurocube architecture shown on the "Stacked 3D chips" slide.
